notes.front: What is compliance, in the information security sense, in one sentence?
notes.back: Making sure a business meets the regulatory and legal requirements that apply to its data or industry.
notes.explanation: Compliance failures can bring fines and sanctions, on top of any damage the underlying security incident causes.
notes.source: Cloud Native Security Lexicon, “Compliance and Security”
notes.example: Like an annual safety inspection a shop must pass, separate from whether it is actually safe to work in.

notes.front: How do compliance and security differ, in one sentence?
notes.back: Compliance assesses a system against defined requirements with a binary pass/fail outcome; security is the continuous process of managing risk.
notes.explanation: A compliant system is not guaranteed to be secure, nor a secure system guaranteed to be compliant.
notes.source: Cloud Native Security Whitepaper v2, “Security Assurance”
notes.example: Like passing a driving test once, versus actually driving safely every single day afterwards.

notes.front: What is a regulatory framework, in this context, in one sentence?
notes.back: A specific set of legal or industry requirements an organisation must meet to protect the systems it operates.
notes.explanation: Which frameworks apply depends entirely on the organisation's industry and the data it handles.
notes.source: Cloud Native Security Whitepaper v2, “Regulatory Audits”
notes.example: Like different rulebooks for a hospital, a bank and a school, even though all three keep records.
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · frameworks and their scope as of that date

notes.front: What are CIS Benchmarks, in one sentence?
notes.back: Hardening checklists for many products, including Kubernetes, agreed by security experts.
notes.explanation: They represent agreement among many security practitioners, not one vendor's opinion.
notes.source: CIS Benchmarks page
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words
notes.example: Like a checklist agreed by many locksmiths for what “well secured” actually means.
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · CIS Benchmarks page as of that date

notes.front: What is kube-bench, in one sentence?
notes.back: A tool that checks whether Kubernetes is deployed securely by running the checks in the CIS Kubernetes Benchmark.
notes.explanation: It turns a lengthy written benchmark into an automated, repeatable scan of an actual cluster.
notes.source: kube-bench README
notes.example: Like a home inspector who checks a house against a published safety standard, item by item.

notes.front: What is NIST SP 800-190, in one sentence?
notes.back: NIST's Application Container Security Guide (September 2017), covering risks and countermeasures across the container lifecycle.
notes.explanation: It is one of the few compliance benchmarks the whitepaper names by title, and predates Kubernetes-specific guidance.
notes.source: NIST SP 800-190
notes.example: Like a general handbook on securing shipping containers, written before container ships specialised further.

notes.front: What is the Secure Software Development Framework (SSDF), in one sentence?
notes.back: A NIST framework (SP 800-218) of secure development practices, which the whitepaper maps to the cloud native lifecycle.
notes.explanation: SSDF is about how software is built; SLSA gives one way to measure how well a supply chain lives up to it.
notes.source: Cloud Native Security Whitepaper v2, “SSDF v1.1 Mapping”
notes.example: Like a recipe standard for how a kitchen should be run, not a rating of any one dish.

notes.front: What is the NSA/CISA Kubernetes Hardening Guidance, in one sentence?
notes.back: A U.S. government hardening guide for Kubernetes, with versions 1.0, 1.1 and 1.2.
notes.explanation: It is a government-produced companion to vendor-neutral benchmarks like CIS, covering broadly the same ground from a different source.
notes.source: Kubernetes blog, “A Closer Look at NSA/CISA Kubernetes Hardening Guidance”
notes.example: Like a government-issued home security leaflet, alongside an industry-written one covering similar ground.

notes.front: What is OpenSCAP, in one sentence?
notes.back: A compliance benchmark tool named by the whitepaper alongside CIS and NIST guidance.
notes.explanation: It is one more example of automated tooling for checking a system against a written security benchmark.
notes.source: Cloud Native Security Whitepaper v2, “Compliance”
notes.example: Like a third brand of home inspection checklist, alongside two others already in the room.

notes.front: What is the OWASP Kubernetes Top Ten, in one sentence?
notes.back: OWASP's ranked list of the most significant Kubernetes security risks, revised periodically.
notes.explanation: As a ranked list, its exact order and risk names have already changed once between editions, so treat it as volatile.
notes.source: OWASP Kubernetes Top Ten
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words
notes.example: Like an annually updated “most common burglary methods” list for a neighbourhood.
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · both the 2022 and 2025 editions were live on that date

notes.front: What is OCTAVE, in one sentence?
notes.back: A mature, well-used threat modelling method, named by the whitepaper as an alternative to STRIDE.
notes.explanation: It gives teams a second option to STRIDE when picking a systematic way to identify threats.
notes.source: Cloud Native Security Whitepaper v2, “Threat Identification”
notes.example: Like choosing between two well-regarded map styles to plan the same journey.

notes.front: What is the OWASP four-step threat modelling approach, in one sentence?
notes.back: A four-step method the whitepaper's own threat modelling guidance is built as an enhancement of.
notes.explanation: Recognising that the whitepaper's guidance did not appear from nowhere helps place it in the wider threat modelling landscape.
notes.source: Cloud Native Security Whitepaper v2, “Threat Modeling”
notes.example: Like a four-step recipe that a more detailed cookbook chapter later expands on.

notes.front: What is automated governance, in one sentence?
notes.back: Using automation to consistently enforce an organisation's governance policies and security controls, often via Policy as Code.
notes.explanation: It turns compliance and policy checks into quick, automatic feedback in a pipeline, instead of a manual review later.
notes.source: Cloud Native Security Lexicon, “Automated Governance”
notes.example: Like a building's automatic fire door that locks itself shut, rather than relying on a guard to check it daily.

notes.front: What is supply chain compliance, in one sentence?
notes.back: Showing a software supply chain meets requirements; the whitepaper names SBOMs and attestations as the evidence a secure CI/CD system should generate.
notes.explanation: It is where the supply chain security ideas from earlier topics get tied to formal compliance evidence.
notes.source: Cloud Native Security Whitepaper v2, “Supply Chain Security”
notes.example: Like proving a meal's ingredients were sourced properly with receipts, not just tasting good.

notes.front: What is NIST SP 800-204, in one sentence?
notes.back: NIST's security strategies for microservices-based application systems, named by the whitepaper alongside CIS and NIST SP 800-190.
notes.explanation: It extends compliance guidance from container security specifically into the microservices architecture built on top of it.
notes.source: Cloud Native Security Whitepaper v2, “Compliance”
notes.example: Like a follow-up handbook for the systems built on top of the containers the first handbook covered.

notes.front: What is the US Executive Order on cybersecurity of May 2021, in one sentence?
notes.back: A US order that pushed for hardening the software supply chain, cited by SLSA as the reason a shared framework was needed.
notes.explanation: It is the policy event SLSA itself points to as the reason a shared supply-chain security framework was needed.
notes.source: SLSA specification, “About SLSA”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words
notes.example: Like new building regulations issued after a widely reported structural failure.

notes.front: What kind of outcome does a compliance assessment typically produce?
notes.back: A binary pass/fail outcome, though it may contain Type 1 (false positive) or Type 2 (false negative) errors.
notes.explanation: Treating compliance results like CI/CD pipeline test results helps teams see them as one signal among several, not the final word.
notes.source: Cloud Native Security Whitepaper v2, “Security Assurance”

notes.front: How does security hardening differ in character from a compliance assessment?
notes.back: It is iterative and perpetual, continually evaluating and adjusting components rather than producing a one-off pass or fail.
notes.explanation: The whitepaper calls security "fundamentally a risk management process"; compliance gives a pass or fail.
notes.source: Cloud Native Security Whitepaper v2, “Security Assurance”

notes.front: What are three regulatory frameworks organisations should evaluate against their cloud native systems, and a fourth?
notes.back: The payment card industry standard, the U.S. healthcare privacy law and European data protection law; a U.S. federal cloud authorisation programme is a fourth.
notes.explanation: Which of these apply depends entirely on the organisation's industry and the data it processes.
notes.source: Cloud Native Security Whitepaper v2, “Regulatory Audits”

notes.front: How should organisations gather evidence that they meet a regulatory standard's requirements?
notes.back: Through an automated evidence-gathering mechanism with non-repudiation guarantees wherever possible.
notes.explanation: Automated, non-repudiable evidence is far more defensible in an audit than a manually assembled report.
notes.source: Cloud Native Security Whitepaper v2, “Regulatory Audits”

notes.front: What can't CIS Benchmarks and similar hardening benchmarks account for, according to the whitepaper?
notes.back: Data flows and custom usage of the platforms under testing; they should guide, not replace, judgement.
notes.explanation: The whitepaper explicitly warns to treat benchmarks as a guide rather than a checklist for this reason.
notes.source: Cloud Native Security Whitepaper v2, “Compliance”

notes.front: Is there a one-to-one mapping between Kubernetes releases and CIS Kubernetes Benchmark releases?
notes.back: No: kube-bench's own documentation says there is not, and points to a support table for which release covers which.
notes.explanation: This means a cluster's Kubernetes version and its applicable CIS Benchmark version must be checked separately.
notes.source: kube-bench README

notes.front: What five areas does NIST SP 800-190 cover risks and countermeasures for?
notes.back: Images, registries, orchestrators, containers and the container-specific host operating system.
notes.explanation: This scope is why NIST SP 800-190 is cited across several topics in this deck, from image scanning to isolation.
notes.source: NIST SP 800-190

notes.front: When was NIST SP 800-190 published, and how long is it?
notes.back: September 2017, 63 pages.
notes.explanation: Being from 2017, it predates many later Kubernetes-specific security features, so it is used for general container risk concepts.
notes.source: NIST SP 800-190 title page

notes.front: How does SLSA relate to the SSDF?
notes.back: SLSA levels give a yardstick for how well an organisation's practices measure up against the SSDF.
notes.explanation: This links two ideas taught in different topics: SLSA's build levels and the SSDF's development practices.
notes.source: SLSA specification, “About SLSA”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What does the whitepaper's SSDF v1.1 Mapping table do?
notes.back: It maps each stage of the cloud native application lifecycle to specific SSDF practices and tasks.
notes.explanation: This mapping is what lets a team show, stage by stage, how their existing lifecycle practices satisfy SSDF requirements.
notes.source: Cloud Native Security Whitepaper v2, “SSDF v1.1 Mapping”

notes.front: What are the three published versions of the NSA/CISA Kubernetes Hardening Guidance, and when did each appear?
notes.back: Version 1.0 (August 2021), version 1.1 (March 2022, after industry feedback), and version 1.2 (August 2022, corrections and clarifications).
notes.explanation: Version 1.2 (August 2022) is the latest the Kubernetes blog records.
notes.source: Kubernetes blog, “A Closer Look at NSA/CISA Kubernetes Hardening Guidance”

notes.front: Does the NSA/CISA hardening guidance use the same control plane port numbers as the current Kubernetes documentation?
notes.back: No: the Kubernetes blog notes that kube-scheduler and kube-controller-manager use different ports than the guidance mentions.
notes.explanation: When the two disagree on a detail like a port number, the current Kubernetes documentation should be treated as authoritative.
notes.source: Kubernetes blog, “A Closer Look at NSA/CISA Kubernetes Hardening Guidance”
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · as noted on the Kubernetes blog on that date

notes.front: How many editions of the OWASP Kubernetes Top Ten are currently live, and do their risk orders match?
notes.back: Two: a 2022 edition and a 2025 edition, with different risk orders and some renamed risks.
notes.explanation: Because both editions are live at once, a card that quotes a risk's rank number would quickly go stale or be ambiguous.
notes.source: OWASP Kubernetes Top Ten
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · both editions live on that date

notes.front: Which two threat models does the whitepaper recommend leveraging for cloud native threat identification?
notes.back: STRIDE and OCTAVE, both described as mature, well-used models.
notes.explanation: Naming two alternatives, rather than mandating one, reflects that threat modelling method is a team's choice.
notes.source: Cloud Native Security Whitepaper v2, “Threat Identification”

notes.front: How does the whitepaper's own threat modelling guidance relate to the OWASP four-step approach?
notes.back: It is described as an enhancement of the OWASP threat modelling approach, adapted for cloud native.
notes.explanation: This means the whitepaper's guidance builds on, rather than replaces, an existing, widely used method.
notes.source: Cloud Native Security Whitepaper v2, “Threat Modeling”

notes.front: What tool does the lexicon give as an example for implementing automated governance?
notes.back: Open Policy Agent, aligning automated policy enforcement with organisational objectives.
notes.explanation: Open Policy Agent is one concrete way to turn a written policy into an automated check enforced in a pipeline or cluster.
notes.source: Cloud Native Security Lexicon, “Automated Governance”

notes.front: What should a secure CI/CD system generate, as evidence for supply chain compliance?
notes.back: SBOMs and attestations.
notes.explanation: Each piece of evidence covers a different question: what's in the software, and how it was built.
notes.source: Cloud Native Security Whitepaper v2, “Supply Chain Security”

notes.front: What specific event does SLSA cite as affirming the need for a universal software supply chain framework?
notes.back: The US Executive Order on Improving the Nation's Cybersecurity, of 12 May 2021.
notes.explanation: SLSA points to this order as part of the case for why a shared, incrementally adoptable framework was needed.
notes.source: SLSA specification, “About SLSA”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What does NIST SP 800-204 provide security strategies for?
notes.back: Microservices-based application systems.
notes.explanation: It sits alongside NIST SP 800-190 as one of the benchmarks the whitepaper lists for compliance.
notes.source: Cloud Native Security Whitepaper v2, “Compliance”

notes.front: A payment processor must protect cardholder data across its Kubernetes-hosted checkout service. Which regulatory framework applies most directly?
notes.back: The payment card industry standard.
notes.choices:
A) The payment card industry standard
B) The U.S. healthcare privacy law
C) European data protection law
notes.choicesExplained: B: the healthcare privacy law covers patient health records, not payment cards. C: European data protection law covers personal data broadly, not payment cards specifically.
notes.explanation: Each regulatory framework targets a specific industry or jurisdiction: payment cards, healthcare, European data, or US government cloud services.
notes.source: Cloud Native Security Whitepaper v2, “Regulatory Audits”

notes.front: A hospital's Kubernetes cluster stores patient health records. Which regulatory framework applies most directly?
notes.back: The U.S. healthcare privacy law.
notes.choices:
A) The U.S. healthcare privacy law
B) The payment card industry standard
C) European data protection law
notes.choicesExplained: B: the payment card industry standard covers cardholder data, not health records. C: European data protection law covers personal data broadly, not this US healthcare-specific case.
notes.explanation: Each regulatory framework targets a specific industry or jurisdiction: payment cards, healthcare, European data, or US government cloud services.
notes.source: Cloud Native Security Whitepaper v2, “Regulatory Audits”

notes.front: A company processes the personal data of European residents in its cluster. Which regulatory framework applies most directly?
notes.back: European data protection law.
notes.choices:
A) European data protection law
B) The U.S. healthcare privacy law
C) FedRAMP
notes.choicesExplained: B: the healthcare privacy law covers US health data, not general European personal data. C: FedRAMP covers US federal cloud services, unrelated to this scenario.
notes.explanation: Each regulatory framework targets a specific industry or jurisdiction: payment cards, healthcare, European data, or US government cloud services.
notes.source: Cloud Native Security Whitepaper v2, “Regulatory Audits”

notes.front: A vendor wants to offer its Kubernetes-based service to the U.S. federal government. Which regulatory framework applies most directly?
notes.back: FedRAMP.
notes.choices:
A) FedRAMP
B) The payment card industry standard
C) European data protection law
notes.choicesExplained: B: the payment card industry standard covers payment cards, not federal cloud authorisation. C: European data protection law covers personal data, not US federal procurement.
notes.explanation: Each regulatory framework targets a specific industry or jurisdiction: payment cards, healthcare, European data, or US government cloud services.
notes.source: Cloud Native Security Whitepaper v2, “Regulatory Audits”

notes.front: A cluster passes every CIS Benchmark check, yet is compromised through a business-logic flaw the benchmark never tested. What does this best illustrate?
notes.back: That a compliant system is not guaranteed to be secure; compliance and security assurance are complementary but not interchangeable.
notes.choices:
A) A compliant system is not guaranteed to be secure
B) The CIS Benchmark must have been applied incorrectly
C) Business-logic flaws cannot occur in a compliant system
notes.choicesExplained: B: passing a benchmark correctly does not mean every possible flaw was covered by it. C: benchmarks check configuration, not application-specific business logic.
notes.explanation: Compliance benchmarks check known, generic configuration issues; they were never designed to catch every application-specific flaw.
notes.source: Cloud Native Security Whitepaper v2, “Security Assurance”

notes.front: A team wants an automated, repeatable way to check a live cluster against the CIS Kubernetes Benchmark before every release. What tool fits this need?
notes.back: kube-bench, which runs the CIS Kubernetes Benchmark's checks against the cluster automatically.
notes.choices:
A) kube-bench
B) Falco
C) cosign
notes.choicesExplained: B: Falco detects runtime behaviour anomalies, not benchmark configuration compliance. C: cosign verifies signatures on artefacts, unrelated to benchmark compliance.
notes.explanation: kube-bench exists specifically to automate what would otherwise be a manual, error-prone benchmark check.
notes.source: kube-bench README

notes.front: An auditor asks a team to demonstrate their build pipeline's maturity against the Secure Software Development Framework. What evidence would help make that case?
notes.back: Their measured SLSA Build level, since SLSA gives a yardstick for progress on SSDF practices.
notes.choices:
A) Their measured SLSA Build level
B) Their CIS Benchmark score
C) Their Pod Security Standard level
notes.choicesExplained: B: a CIS Benchmark score reflects cluster configuration, not build pipeline maturity. C: Pod Security Standards govern workload configuration at runtime, not the build process.
notes.explanation: SLSA is explicitly positioned as a way to measure how well a supply chain meets SSDF practices.
notes.source: SLSA specification, “About SLSA”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: A team wants every commit that violates their security policy to be blocked automatically, without a human reviewing each one. What practice does this describe?
notes.back: Automated governance, typically implemented with Policy as Code tooling such as Open Policy Agent.
notes.choices:
A) Automated governance
B) Manual regulatory audit
C) Threat modelling
notes.choicesExplained: B: a manual audit is, by definition, not automatic. C: threat modelling identifies risks; it does not by itself enforce policy automatically.
notes.explanation: Automated governance is exactly this: using automation to consistently enforce policies, with quick feedback built into the workflow.
notes.source: Cloud Native Security Lexicon, “Automated Governance”

notes.front: A team follows the NSA/CISA hardening guidance's stated port numbers for kube-scheduler and finds they don't match the live cluster. What should they do?
notes.back: Trust the current Kubernetes documentation, since the blog notes the guidance uses different port numbers than Kubernetes actually does.
notes.choices:
A) Trust the current Kubernetes documentation over the guidance
B) Assume their cluster is misconfigured
C) Disable kube-scheduler entirely
notes.choicesExplained: B: the mismatch is a known discrepancy in the guidance, not a sign of misconfiguration. C: disabling a control plane component is not a reasonable response to a documentation mismatch.
notes.explanation: This is a documented discrepancy: use the authoritative, currently maintained Kubernetes documentation when the two disagree.
notes.source: Kubernetes blog, “A Closer Look at NSA/CISA Kubernetes Hardening Guidance”

notes.front: Why check which edition an OWASP Kubernetes Top Ten rank number comes from, before quoting it?
notes.back: Because two editions (2022 and 2025) are live with different orders and renamed risks, so a rank number alone can be ambiguous or outdated.
notes.choices:
A) The rank number is ambiguous between live editions
B) OWASP does not rank its risks
C) Rank numbers never change between editions
notes.choicesExplained: B: OWASP does present both lists as ranked, numbered risks. C: the two live editions disagree on order, which is exactly the problem.
notes.explanation: With two live editions disagreeing on order, only the risk names themselves, not their rank numbers, are safe to treat as stable facts.
notes.source: OWASP Kubernetes Top Ten
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What should a secure CI/CD system generate, so a team can demonstrate supply chain compliance?
notes.back: SBOMs and attestations.
notes.choices:
A) SBOMs and attestations
B) Only a signed build attestation
C) Only an SBOM
notes.choicesExplained: B and C: the whitepaper names both together, not either alone.
notes.explanation: Supply chain compliance is built from several complementary pieces of evidence, not any single artefact.
notes.source: Cloud Native Security Whitepaper v2, “Supply Chain Security”

notes.front: How do compliance and security differ as ideas?
notes.back: Compliance is a binary pass/fail assessment against defined requirements; security is the continuous, iterative process of managing risk.
notes.explanation: The whitepaper: "A compliant system is not guaranteed to be secure, nor a secure system is guaranteed to be compliant."
notes.source: Cloud Native Security Whitepaper v2, “Security Assurance”

notes.front: How do CIS Benchmarks and kube-bench differ?
notes.back: CIS Benchmarks are the written, consensus-based recommendations; kube-bench is a tool that automates checking a cluster against them.
notes.explanation: One is a standard to read; the other is software that checks a live system against that standard.
notes.source: kube-bench README / CIS Benchmarks page

notes.front: How does STRIDE differ from OCTAVE, as the whitepaper presents them?
notes.back: The whitepaper does not contrast them: both are named as mature, well-used models, with the choice left to the team.
notes.explanation: Neither STRIDE nor OCTAVE is prescribed over the other; the whitepaper leaves the choice to the team.
notes.source: Cloud Native Security Whitepaper v2, “Threat Identification”

notes.front: How do the OWASP Kubernetes Top Ten's 2022 and 2025 editions differ?
notes.back: Both list ten Kubernetes risks, but with different orders and some risks renamed or reorganised between editions.
notes.explanation: This is why the deck treats OWASP Top Ten rank numbers as volatile and cards only the risk names as stable facts.
notes.source: OWASP Kubernetes Top Ten
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: A security review wants to check for embedded clear-text secrets and untrusted base images in a container image, before it is used. Which compliance benchmark covers exactly this risk area?
notes.back: NIST SP 800-190: it lists image vulnerabilities, configuration defects and embedded secrets as image risks.
notes.choices:
A) NIST SP 800-190
B) The OWASP Kubernetes Top Ten
C) The NSA/CISA Kubernetes Hardening Guidance
notes.choicesExplained: B: OWASP's list ranks broader Kubernetes risks, not the detailed image-risk breakdown NIST SP 800-190 gives. C: the hardening guidance focuses on cluster configuration, not image content risks specifically.
notes.explanation: NIST SP 800-190 devotes a specific section to image risks, including embedded secrets and untrusted images, making it the most direct fit.
notes.source: NIST SP 800-190
